body:
What is nanotechnology?

Nanotechnology is the understanding, manipulation and use of matter at extremely small dimensions, generally between approximately 1 and 100 nanometres, where materials may exhibit properties different from those of the same substance in its larger form.

A nanometre (nm) is one-billionth of a metre. Thus, 1 nm equals 0.000000001 metre. The prefix nano indicates a scale, not a particular chemical substance. Gold, carbon, silver and many other materials can have nanoscale forms.

Nanoscience studies the behaviour of matter at this scale. Nanotechnology applies that understanding to develop useful materials, devices and processes.

Nanomaterial: A material with at least one external dimension or an internal or surface structure in the nanoscale, according to the definition applicable to that material. A nanoparticle generally has all 3 external dimensions in the nanoscale.

Why can properties change at the nanoscale?

Greater surface area relative to volume

When a solid material is divided into many smaller particles, more of its atoms become exposed at the surface. For the same mass, smaller particles usually provide a larger total surface area than larger pieces of the same material.

Surface atoms can interact with surrounding substances. Therefore, a larger exposed surface can improve adsorption, catalysis or chemical reactivity in suitable materials. This is one reason nanoparticles are investigated for water purification, pollution control and chemical sensors.

Changes in optical and electronic behaviour

At sufficiently small dimensions, the movement and energy of electrons can be affected by the size and structure of a material. This is associated with quantum effects. For example, certain semiconductor nanoparticles emit different colours of light depending on their size.

Other properties, including strength, electrical conductivity and magnetism, can also change with size and structure. However, the direction and extent of change depend on the material. Every nanoscale substance does not become stronger, more conductive or more reactive.

Natural, incidental and engineered nanoparticles

Nanoscale particles are not exclusively human inventions. Some occur naturally, while others are produced unintentionally by human activities.

  • Natural nanoparticles: Nanoscale particles produced by processes such as volcanic activity or natural mineral formation.
  • Incidental nanoparticles: Particles generated unintentionally, for example in combustion smoke or welding fumes.
  • Engineered nanoparticles: Particles deliberately manufactured or modified to obtain particular properties or functions.

This distinction matters because a particle's origin, chemical composition and use affect how it should be studied and controlled.

Nanotechnology is broader than nanoparticles

A nanotechnology product need not consist of loose nanoparticles. It may contain nanoparticles embedded in a larger material, a very thin coating, a membrane with nanoscale features, or a miniature electronic sensing structure.

For instance, a coating containing nanoscale particles and a bottle containing a suspension of free nanoparticles may involve similar substances but create different opportunities for human exposure.

Prelims focus

  • 1 nm equals 10-9 metre.
  • Nanotechnology commonly concerns dimensions of approximately 1-100 nm.
  • A higher surface-area-to-volume ratio can increase interactions between a material and its surroundings.
  • Some nanoscale materials exhibit size-dependent optical or electronic properties.
  • Natural, incidental and engineered nanoparticles are distinct categories.
  • Trap: Nanoscale size alone does not establish that a material is useful, toxic or safe.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapters Atoms and Molecules and Structure of the Atom; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, About Nanotechnology, sections How Small Is Nano? and What Is Special About Nano?, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Nanotechnology: Meaning, Scale and Basic Principles

body:
Nanomaterials are classified by their structure and composition

Nanotechnology uses many different substances. Their usefulness comes from the combination of chemical composition, size, shape and surface characteristics.

A nanoscale material may be a small particle, an extremely thin sheet, a narrow tube, or part of a larger composite. The shape determines which dimensions are small and how the material interacts with its surroundings.

Common examples

NanomaterialImportant propertyRepresentative use
Silver nanoparticlesAntimicrobial activity under suitable conditionsSelected antimicrobial coatings and materials
Titanium dioxide nanoparticlesUltraviolet interaction and, in suitable forms, photocatalytic activitySunscreens and photocatalytic surfaces
Zinc oxide nanoparticlesAbsorption and scattering of ultraviolet radiationSelected sunscreen formulations
Carbon nanotubesHigh strength and useful electrical properties in suitable formsComposites and electronic components
GrapheneExtremely thin carbon sheet with notable electrical and mechanical propertiesResearch and development in sensors and electronics
Semiconductor quantum dotsSize-dependent optical behaviourDisplay technologies and optical applications
Lipid nanoparticlesAbility to carry and protect certain substancesDelivery of selected medicines and biological molecules

Particles, tubes, sheets and coatings

A nanoparticle typically has nanoscale dimensions in all 3 spatial directions. A nanotube has a very small diameter but can be much longer. A nanosheet has nanoscale thickness while its length and width can be much larger. A nanocoating is a thin surface layer or a coating that contains nanoscale structures.

Graphene is a well-known example of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a 2-dimensional structure. Carbon nanotubes can be understood conceptually as cylindrical carbon structures with nanoscale diameters.

Nanocomposites and free nanoparticles

A nanocomposite combines a larger material, such as a polymer, with a nanoscale component to modify its properties. For example, incorporating suitable carbon nanomaterials into a polymer can change the strength or electrical behaviour of the resulting material.

The nanoparticles in a nanocomposite may remain attached within the larger material. Free nanoparticles, in contrast, can be dispersed in air or liquid. This difference becomes important when considering environmental release and occupational exposure.

How are nanostructures produced?

Two broad approaches describe nanomaterial production:

  • Top-down approach: A larger material is reduced or patterned to obtain smaller structures. The essential idea is to begin with bulk matter and create smaller features.
  • Bottom-up approach: Atoms, molecules or small building blocks are assembled into a desired nanoscale structure.

These terms describe the general direction of material formation. Neither method by itself guarantees a particular level of product quality or safety.

A nanomaterial's chemical identity remains important. Silver nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes and lipid nanoparticles do not have the same properties or toxicological behaviour merely because they are nanoscale.

Connecting material properties with applications

Useful applications depend on matching a material's specific property with a task. Optical behaviour is useful in displays; electrical changes can support sensing; surface interactions may assist purification; and carrier properties can support drug delivery.

The correct reasoning is therefore material and structure, followed by property, followed by possible application. The presence of the prefix nano is not sufficient evidence of improved performance.

Prelims focus

  • Graphene is a 2-dimensional carbon material.
  • Carbon nanotubes have nanoscale diameters and can be much longer than their diameters.
  • Quantum dots can exhibit size-dependent optical properties.
  • Titanium dioxide and zinc oxide are used in selected ultraviolet-protective formulations.
  • Top-down means reducing or patterning larger material; bottom-up means assembling smaller building blocks.
  • Trap: A nanocomposite is not necessarily a suspension of free nanoparticles.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter Synthetic Fibres and Plastics, printed pp. 32-36, for polymer and composite foundations; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, About Nanotechnology and Applications of Nanotechnology, sections on materials and consumer products, consulted 13 November 2026; U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Nanotechnology Frequently Asked Questions, updated 3 March 2026.]

title: Types of Nanomaterials and Their Useful Properties

body:
Why are nanomaterials useful in medicine?

Medicines must reach the appropriate part of the body and remain effective while avoiding unacceptable harm. Some drugs break down before reaching their intended site, dissolve poorly, or affect healthy tissues as well as diseased tissues.

Nanotechnology can help address some of these difficulties by changing how a medicine is carried, protected or released. It can also improve selected diagnostic methods through very small sensing structures.

Nanocarriers and controlled delivery

A nanocarrier is a nanoscale structure used to transport another substance. The substance carried may be a conventional drug or a biological molecule.

A drug can be enclosed within or associated with a carrier. Depending on its design, the carrier may protect the drug, help it remain dispersed, alter where it travels in the body, or influence the rate at which it is released.

Liposomes are small vesicles made from lipid membranes. Lipid nanoparticles are another group of lipid-based delivery systems. Both are important examples of using lipid structures in medicine, but their internal organisation and applications are not necessarily identical.

Targeted drug delivery

Targeted drug delivery aims to increase the delivery of a treatment to a selected tissue or cell. Some carriers may be designed to interact with particular biological targets.

However, targeting is not perfect or universal. The amount reaching a tissue also depends on circulation, the body's protective barriers, clearance mechanisms and the properties of the carrier. A nanocarrier does not automatically deliver all of its drug to diseased cells.

Examples in medical treatment

  • Cancer treatment: Certain nanoparticle or liposomal formulations can alter the distribution of anticancer medicines. A possible benefit is better treatment delivery or reduced exposure to some healthy tissues, but effectiveness and adverse effects require evaluation for each formulation.
  • Delivery of genetic material: Lipid nanoparticles can carry selected RNA molecules, including those used in some vaccines.
  • Medical coatings: Materials incorporating antimicrobial nanoparticles may help control microbial growth on appropriately designed surfaces or products.

Nanotechnology and genetic engineering are not synonyms. A lipid nanoparticle that carries RNA is a delivery system. Genetic engineering involves deliberate modification or manipulation of genetic material. The carrier itself does not necessarily perform genetic editing.

Nanotechnology in diagnosis

A diagnostic biosensor detects a biological target, such as a protein, and converts the interaction into an observable signal. Nanoparticles can support this process because their optical or electrical properties may change, or because they provide a suitable surface for attaching biological recognition molecules.

Gold nanoparticles are used as visible signal-producing labels in certain rapid diagnostic tests. Their colour-related optical properties help make a biological binding event easier to observe. This is different from using nanoparticles as medicines.

Research also explores nanoscale sensing materials for detecting disease-associated molecules at low concentrations. Detection still depends on the sensitivity, specificity and validation of the complete diagnostic device.

Medical safety and approval

The body can respond differently to a medicine when its particle size, carrier composition, surface or distribution changes. Therefore, a nanopharmaceutical needs assessment of its quality, stability, safety and effectiveness rather than being assumed equivalent to a conventional formulation.

India's Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India, issued in October 2019 by the Department of Biotechnology, Indian Council of Medical Research and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization, address the evaluation of nanopharmaceutical products.

These guidelines provide a scientific evaluation framework. They do not mean that every nanoparticle-based medicine is approved, and they do not replace the applicable statutory drug-approval requirements.

Prelims focus

  • Nanocarriers can protect, transport or modify the release of selected therapeutic substances.
  • Liposomes and lipid nanoparticles are examples of lipid-based delivery systems.
  • Gold nanoparticles can provide visible signals in certain rapid diagnostic tests.
  • Targeted delivery is an objective, not a guarantee of exclusive delivery to diseased tissue.
  • India's nanopharmaceutical evaluation guidelines were issued in October 2019.
  • Trap: Delivering RNA in a nanoparticle is not automatically the same as editing DNA.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapters Biotechnology: Principles and Processes and Biotechnology and Its Applications; Government of India, Department of Biotechnology, Indian Council of Medical Research and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization, Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India, October 2019, sections on quality, safety and efficacy evaluation; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, Applications of Nanotechnology, medical applications section, consulted 13 November 2026.]
